questions.question: Two meadows hold the same 20 species of grasses and wildflowers, with the same number of plants of each. In the first, every plant grew from seed gathered from many wild parents. In the second, all the plants of each species were raised from cuttings of a single parent plant. Which meadow holds more biodiversity?
questions.answer: The first, for the variety in its genes
choices: The first, for the variety in its genes
Neither, for both hold the same 20 species
Neither, for both hold as many plants
Neither, for each species' plants look alike
questions.context: Biodiversity is counted at three levels: the variety of genes within each species, the variety of species, and the variety of ecosystems. A cutting grows into a clone with its parent's genes, while seeds from many parents carry many different mixes of genes, so the first meadow holds far more genetic variety even if its plants look alike. Biodiversity is often taken to mean the number of species alone, but the genes count too.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade's line (G8.L6; NGSS MS-LS2-5) names genetic variety beside species variety as part of biodiversity, and students most often miss the genetic level.

questions.question: David Tilman and John Downing had measured the plant growth in over 200 grassland plots at Cedar Creek, Minnesota, for years when the worst drought in 50 years struck in 1987 and 1988. Plots with more plant species lost a smaller share of their growth. The two then asked how much each lost species weakened a plot against the drought. What did they find?
questions.answer: Each species lost hurt more than the one before it
choices: Each species lost hurt more than the one before it
Each species lost hurt less than the one before it
Each species lost hurt about as much as any other
The first few species lost did no harm at all
questions.context: Drought resistance fell along a curve: a few species lost from a rich plot cost a little, but each further loss cost more, so the plots down to their last few species were hit hardest. Tilman and Downing took this as support for the old idea that diversity brings stability, and against the idea that most species are redundant, doing jobs others already do. Critics noted that nitrogen fertilizer, added to many plots, had cut their species and changed their growth; the two found the pattern held when they allowed for it, though a 2017 reanalysis disputes this.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade's line (G8.L6) teaches that an ecosystem with many species withstands change better and that losing species weakens it; the Cedar Creek drought is the classic evidence.

questions.question: David Tilman followed the plants in 207 grassland plots at Cedar Creek, Minnesota, year after year. In the plots with many species, each species rose and fell in number more from year to year than in plots with few. Yet the total plant mass of those rich plots held steadier. What explains both results?
questions.answer: When some species did badly, others grew to fill in
choices: When some species did badly, others grew to fill in
All of their species rose and fell together each year
Their species stopped competing for water and light
The weather over them swung less from year to year
questions.context: When the weather harms some species, the competitors it spares grow into the room and light they leave, so the plot's total holds steady even as each species swings up and down. The more species a plot holds, the likelier some of them can thrive in any year's weather, which ecologists call the insurance effect. Species that all rose and fell together would make the total swing more, not less.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade's line (G8.L6) asks why an ecosystem with many species withstands change better; if one species fails, others take its place.

questions.question: Blast, a disease caused by a fungus, ravages a prized sticky rice grown in Yunnan, China. Zhu Youyong's team had farmers across whole townships plant single rows of the sticky rice between groups of four or six rows of a hybrid rice that blast seldom harms, in 1998 and 1999. Blast on the sticky rice fell by 94 percent. What best explains the drop?
questions.answer: Most spores now met plants the fungus could not infect
choices: Most spores now met plants the fungus could not infect
The farmers sprayed the mixed fields with more fungicide
The sticky rice caught resistance from the hybrid rice
The hybrid rice took the water the fungus needed
questions.context: Spores from a sick sticky-rice plant now landed mostly on the hybrid rice, which they could not infect, so few reached another sticky-rice plant and the disease could not build up; ecologists call this the dilution effect. By the end of the two years the farmers no longer needed to spray fungicide at all. Resistance is inherited in a plant's genes and is never caught from a neighbour.
questions.grade_note: The unit's scope (G8.L6) teaches that a field of one crop is easy for one disease to sweep, and mixing varieties, the Yunnan trial, is the evidence for genetic variety as protection.

questions.question: The water mould Phytophthora infestans reached Ireland in 1845 and rotted potato fields across the island. Much of the crop was one variety, the Lumper, grown from pieces of its tubers, so every plant carried the same genes, and none could resist late blight, the disease the mould causes. Where did breeders later find genes that let potatoes resist it?
questions.answer: In wild potato species of Mexico
choices: In wild potato species of Mexico
In old potato varieties grown in Ireland
In seedlings raised from the Lumper's seeds
In potatoes sprayed for years against it
questions.context: Early breeders took eleven resistance genes, R1 to R11, from Solanum demissum, a wild potato of Mexico; the mould has since overcome every one, so breeders now stack several, many from other wild species. The variety of genes in a crop's wild relatives is a store that one uniform crop lacks, and Ireland's few varieties had no such resistance to give. Spraying protects a plant but never changes the genes it passes on.
questions.grade_note: The unit's scope (G8.L6) uses Ireland's potato famine as the case of one uniform crop wiped out by one disease, and genetic variety, here in wild relatives, as what protects a crop.

questions.question: Taylor Ricketts' team studied coffee bushes on a large farm in Costa Rica, at sites beside patches of forest and up to 1.6 kilometres away. At each site they dusted some branches' flowers with extra pollen by hand and left other branches alone. Near the forest, both kinds of branch set about the same crop; far from it, the hand-dusted ones set about a fifth more. What did this show?
questions.answer: Bees from the forest reached only the nearer bushes
choices: Bees from the forest reached only the nearer bushes
Water from the forest reached only the nearer bushes
Shade from the forest reached only the nearer bushes
Pests from the forest reached only the nearer bushes
questions.context: Coffee can pollinate itself, but bee visits raise its crop, and the bees that visited it, feral honeybees and ten native kinds of stingless bee, lived in the forest. Far away the flowers got too little pollen, so extra pollen helped; water, shade or pests would have touched both kinds of branch at a site alike. The forest's pollinators raised yields by about 20 percent within a kilometre of it and cut misshapen beans by 27 percent, a service worth about $60,000 a year to the farm.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade's line (G8.L6; NGSS MS-LS2-5) names pollination among the services a diverse ecosystem keeps providing; the coffee trial measures one.

questions.question: Lucas Garibaldi and dozens of colleagues watched crop flowers in 41 crop systems around the world. In each field they counted visits by wild insects and by honeybees from managed hives, and the share of flowers that went on to set fruit. How did the two kinds of visitor compare?
questions.answer: Wild insect visits raised fruit set about twice as much
choices: Wild insect visits raised fruit set about twice as much
Honeybee visits raised fruit set about twice as much
Both kinds of visit raised fruit set about equally
Wild insects mattered only where honeybees were few
questions.context: More visits by wild insects went with more fruit in all 41 systems, while more honeybee visits raised fruit set clearly in only 14 percent of them, and an equal rise in wild insect visits helped twice as much. Wild insects helped whether honeybees were many or few, so the authors concluded that hives add to the work of wild pollinators rather than replacing it.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade's line (G8.L6) teaches that losing biodiversity weakens the services an ecosystem gives, pollination among them; this study weighs wild pollinators against managed hives.

questions.question: American farmers in 1970 planted many different corn hybrids, each grown from seed of a cross between two inbred parent lines. That summer a new race of a fungus, race T, spread through the Corn Belt and cut the country's corn harvest by about 15 percent. Why could one race of fungus harm so many different hybrids?
questions.answer: Most carried the same inherited trait that race T attacked
choices: Most carried the same inherited trait that race T attacked
Every hybrid had been grown from copies of one plant
Race T could attack every kind of corn equally
Race T had built up in the fields for decades
questions.context: To make hybrid seed without pulling off the tassels by hand, seed companies had bred a trait called Texas male-sterile cytoplasm into about 85 to 90 percent of American hybrids, and race T's poison struck corn with that trait in particular. Corn without it held up, and as seed companies went back to normal cytoplasm the danger passed by 1972; race T had first appeared only in 1969. Hybrids that differ in many genes can still share one weakness.
questions.grade_note: The unit's scope (G8.L6) teaches that a crop with little genetic variety is easy for one disease to sweep; the 1970 corn blight shows the uniformity can hide inside many named varieties.

questions.question: Short experiments, most about two years long, had found that more than six or eight plant species in a grassland plot gave no further benefit. Peter Reich's team followed plots at Cedar Creek, Minnesota, sown with 1 to 16 prairie species, for more than a decade. What did they find?
questions.answer: Each added species raised soil fertility and plant growth
choices: Each added species raised soil fertility and plant growth
Species beyond the first eight still added nothing
The richest plots grew less as their plants crowded in
The extra species helped only in years of drought
questions.context: Over the years every added species, up to 16, brought a gradual rise in both the soil's fertility and the plants' growth, because different species gather water, nutrients and carbon in different ways and hold them in the ecosystem. The short experiments had ended before these gains built up, so species that seem spare for a year or two prove their worth over a decade, and losing them costs more than a short study can show.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade's line (G8.L6) teaches that losing biodiversity weakens an ecosystem and its services, fertile soil among them; Cedar Creek's long experiments are the evidence.
